questions.title: Exchange of nuclear material between two protozoa
questions.question: Exchange of nuclear materials between two protozoa is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Syngamy is the fusion of two gametes to form a zygote, not the exchange of nuclear material between two organisms.
explanations.B: Correct. Conjugation is a form of sexual reproduction in ciliate protozoa (such as Balantidium coli) in which two organisms temporarily join and exchange micronuclear (nuclear) material before separating. It is the reciprocal transfer of nuclear material that defines the process. This distinguishes conjugation from the other listed processes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gamogony is the formation of gametes, not the exchange of nuclear material.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Budding is an asexual mode of reproduction and involves no exchange of nuclear material.

questions.learning_objective: Define conjugation as the exchange of nuclear material between two protozoa.

questions.title: Protozoan causing granulomatous reactions
questions.question: Granulomatous reactions may occur in infection with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cyclospora causes a watery diarrhoeal illness, not a granulomatous reaction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Giardia is a non-invasive luminal parasite of the small bowel and does not form granulomas.
explanations.C: Correct. Chronic invasive intestinal amoebiasis due to Entamoeba histolytica can produce an amoeboma, a granulomatous tumour-like mass of granulation tissue in the bowel wall that may mimic carcinoma. This granulomatous reaction is a recognised complication of invasive amoebiasis. The other listed protozoa do not form intestinal granulomas.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Naegleria fowleri causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, not intestinal granulomas.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise Entamoeba histolytica as the cause of a granulomatous amoeboma.

questions.title: Haemolytic anaemia in pathogenesis
questions.question: Haemolytic anaemia is involved in the pathogenesis of:

explanations.A: Correct. Malaria produces anaemia chiefly through haemolysis: intra-erythrocytic Plasmodium schizonts rupture infected red cells at the end of each erythrocytic cycle, and immune and splenic clearance also destroys uninfected cells. The result is a haemolytic anaemia. This is the mechanism of malarial anaemia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hookworm causes a chronic iron-deficiency anaemia from intestinal blood loss, not a haemolytic anaemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Schistosomiasis causes anaemia mainly through chronic blood loss and inflammation, not haemolysis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Diphyllobothrium latum causes a megaloblastic (vitamin B12-deficiency) anaemia, not a haemolytic one.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute the anaemia of malaria to haemolysis.

questions.title: Not transmitted through a cystic stage
questions.question: The following is NOT transmitted through a cystic stage:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Giardia lamblia forms a resistant cyst that is the transmissible faecal-oral stage.
explanations.B: Correct. Trichomonas vaginalis exists only as a trophozoite and has no cyst stage, so it cannot survive long outside the host and is transmitted directly, chiefly by sexual contact, rather than through a resistant cyst. The absence of a cyst distinguishes it from the other three. It is therefore the organism not transmitted through a cystic stage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Balantidium coli forms a cyst that mediates faecal-oral transmission.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cryptosporidium parvum is transmitted by a thick-walled oocyst shed in stool.

questions.learning_objective: State that Trichomonas vaginalis lacks a cyst stage.

questions.title: True statement on complications of malaria
questions.question: As regards complications of malaria, the following is true:

options.A: Blackwater fever is the result of cytoadherence of RBCs
options.B: Infection with Plasmodium falciparum may end up with multiorgan failure
options.C: Nephrotic syndrome is a common complication of infection with Plasmodium vivax
options.D: Hyper-reactive malarial splenomegaly is associated with an elevation of serum IgG

explanations.A: Incorrect. Blackwater fever results from massive intravascular haemolysis of red cells, not from cytoadherence.
explanations.B: Correct. Plasmodium falciparum causes severe, complicated malaria and can progress to multiorgan failure because its infected red cells cytoadhere and sequester in the microvasculature of the brain, kidney and lung. This sequestration underlies cerebral, renal and pulmonary complications. Multiorgan failure is therefore a recognised outcome of severe falciparum malaria.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome is a complication of chronic Plasmodium malariae infection, not of P. vivax.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hyper-reactive malarial splenomegaly is associated with elevated serum IgM, not IgG.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise multiorgan failure as a complication of Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

questions.title: True statement on in vitro culture methods
questions.question: As regards in vitro culture methods, the following is true:

options.B: Stool culture for 48 hours yields filariform larvae of Strongyloides
options.C: Culture on NNN medium reveals trypomastigotes of Trypanosoma cruzi
options.D: Culture on modified Diamond's medium yields trophozoites of Trichomonas vaginalis

explanations.A: Incorrect. Culture of Leishmania (for example on NNN medium) yields promastigotes, the flagellated insect-stage form, not amastigotes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Filariform larvae of Strongyloides develop in faecal culture (Harada-Mori) but over about a week, not reliably in 48 hours, and this is not the true statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. NNN culture of trypanosomes yields the insect (epimastigote/promastigote) stages, not blood trypomastigotes of T. cruzi.
explanations.D: Correct. In-vitro culture on modified Diamond's medium is used to grow Trichomonas vaginalis, which appears as motile trophozoites. Diamond's medium is the standard culture system for this flagellate. Culture yielding Trichomonas trophozoites is therefore the true statement.

questions.learning_objective: Match modified Diamond's medium to culture of Trichomonas vaginalis trophozoites.

questions.title: Cause of high IgM in Trypanosoma brucei infection
questions.question: High level of IgM in Trypanosoma brucei infection is due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The IgM rise is not primarily a hypersensitivity reaction.
explanations.B: Correct. African trypanosomes repeatedly change their variant surface glycoprotein coat by antigenic variation, so the host mounts wave after wave of new antibody responses, producing the very high polyclonal IgM levels characteristic of sleeping sickness. The IgM elevation reflects this continual antigenic switching. Antigenic variation is therefore the cause of the raised IgM.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Trypanosoma brucei does not produce microfilariae; that stage belongs to the filarial nematodes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The high IgM is driven by antigenic variation, not by an autoimmune reaction.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute the high IgM of Trypanosoma brucei infection to antigenic variation.

questions.title: When malaria shows no relapse
questions.question: Malaria infection with no relapse occurs when:

options.D: There's mixed infection with different species

explanations.A: Correct. Relapse is caused by dormant liver hypnozoites of Plasmodium vivax and ovale, which form only when sporozoites are inoculated by a mosquito bite. In transplacental (congenital) malaria the fetus receives blood-stage parasites directly across the placenta, so no liver stage and no hypnozoites are established, and the infection cannot relapse. Transplacental transmission therefore gives malaria with no relapse.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Immunosuppression does not remove hypnozoites and is not the reason for absence of relapse.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Incomplete treatment tends to permit recrudescence or relapse, not to abolish relapse.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mixed-species infection does not explain the absence of relapse.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that transplacentally transmitted malaria does not relapse.

questions.title: Parasite causing destruction of nasal cartilage
questions.question: Which of the following parasites causes destruction of nasal cartilage?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Leishmania donovani causes visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), not destruction of nasal cartilage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Leishmania infantum causes visceral (and some cutaneous) disease, not mucocutaneous cartilage destruction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leishmania tropica causes localised cutaneous leishmaniasis (oriental sore), which does not destroy nasal cartilage.
explanations.D: Correct. Leishmania braziliensis causes mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (espundia), in which metastatic spread to the naso-oropharyngeal mucosa produces destructive, disfiguring lesions that erode the nasal septum and cartilage. This mucosal metastasis is characteristic of the species. Destruction of nasal cartilage therefore points to L. braziliensis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify L. braziliensis as the cause of nasal cartilage destruction.

questions.title: Species with fine malaria pigment
questions.question: Fine malaria pigment is found in RBCs infected with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Plasmodium falciparum shows one or two blocks of dark pigment in its gametocytes, not the fine scattered pigment of vivax.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Plasmodium ovale is not the species characterised by fine pigment in this comparison.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Plasmodium malariae characteristically produces coarse, dark pigment, the opposite of fine pigment.
explanations.D: Correct. Plasmodium vivax produces a fine, scattered, light-brown malaria pigment (haemozoin) in the infected red cell, in contrast to the coarse dark pigment of P. malariae. Recognising fine pigment alongside an enlarged red cell with Schuffner dots helps identify P. vivax on a film. Fine pigment is therefore characteristic of P. vivax.

questions.learning_objective: Associate fine malaria pigment with Plasmodium vivax.

questions.title: Finding that confirms babesiosis
questions.question: To confirm diagnosis of babesiosis, we should detect:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ring stages in red cells occur in Babesia but closely resemble Plasmodium falciparum rings, so they are not confirmatory.
explanations.B: Correct. Babesia multiplies inside red cells and can form a tetrad of four merozoites arranged as a Maltese cross, which is pathognomonic and confirms babesiosis on a stained blood film. This tetrad distinguishes Babesia from the ring-only forms of Plasmodium. Detecting the Maltese cross therefore confirms the diagnosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Babesia does not present diagnostic sporozoites within red cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Babesia has no exo-erythrocytic liver stage, so liver-cell merozoites are not seen.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the Maltese-cross tetrad as confirmatory of babesiosis.

questions.title: Malaria species causing nephrotic syndrome
questions.question: Nephrotic syndrome occurs as a complication of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Plasmodium ovale is not associated with the immune-complex nephropathy of quartan malaria.
explanations.B: Correct. Chronic Plasmodium malariae (quartan) infection can cause an immune-complex glomerulonephritis that presents as nephrotic syndrome, classically in children (quartan malarial nephropathy). Immune complexes deposit in the glomerular basement membrane as a type III reaction. Nephrotic syndrome is therefore a complication specific to P. malariae.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Plasmodium falciparum causes acute renal failure from tubular necrosis, not the nephrotic syndrome of quartan nephropathy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Plasmodium vivax is not the species that causes nephrotic syndrome.

questions.learning_objective: Identify nephrotic syndrome as a complication of Plasmodium malariae.

questions.title: Complication of Acanthamoeba keratitis in AIDS
questions.question: Acanthamoeba keratitis in AIDS patients can cause:

explanations.A: Correct. Acanthamoeba keratitis is a sight-threatening corneal infection, and in an immunocompromised (AIDS) patient it can extend beyond the cornea to cause endophthalmitis. This is a local ocular complication arising directly from the keratitis. Endophthalmitis is therefore the ocular complication produced by the keratitis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Granulomatous amoebic encephalitis is a separate disseminated CNS disease of Acanthamoeba, not a direct sequel of keratitis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acanthamoeba does not cause gastroenteritis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Respiratory tract infection is not the ocular complication asked about here.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise endophthalmitis as an ocular complication of Acanthamoeba keratitis.

questions.title: Infection from swimming in contaminated water
questions.question: Swimming in contaminated water can cause infection with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acanthamoeba usually enters through skin, cornea (contact lenses) or the respiratory route, not chiefly by swimming.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Toxoplasma is acquired by ingesting oocysts or tissue cysts, not by swimming.
explanations.C: Correct. Naegleria fowleri is a free-living amoeba of warm fresh water, and infection follows swimming or diving in contaminated water when the amoebae enter the nose and cross the cribriform plate to cause primary amoebic meningoencephalitis. Swimming is the classic exposure. Contaminated-water swimming therefore points to Naegleria fowleri.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dracunculus medinensis is acquired by drinking water containing infected Cyclops, not by swimming.

questions.learning_objective: Link swimming in contaminated fresh water to Naegleria fowleri.

questions.title: True statement on Acanthamoeba keratitis
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding Acanthamoeba keratitis?

options.A: For isolation of the causative agent, corneal scraping is not reliable
options.B: The causative agent, Acanthamoeba, is a helminth whose normal habitat is soil
options.C: Keratitis due to Acanthamoeba is not seen in the immunocompromised host
options.D: Acanthamoeba does not depend upon a human host for the completion of its life cycle

explanations.A: Incorrect. Corneal scraping is in fact a reliable specimen for isolating Acanthamoeba.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acanthamoeba is a free-living protozoan (amoeba), not a helminth, although its habitat does include soil and water.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Keratitis is seen mainly in immunocompetent contact-lens wearers, but Acanthamoeba can also affect the immunocompromised, so this statement is false.
explanations.D: Correct. Acanthamoeba is a free-living amoeba whose normal habitat is soil and water, and it completes its entire life cycle of trophozoite and cyst in the environment without requiring a human host; humans are only accidental hosts. It therefore does not depend on a human host to complete its life cycle. This is the true statement.

questions.learning_objective: State that Acanthamoeba is free-living and needs no human host.

questions.hold: toxoplasmosis immunology ambiguous — printed key B ('IgA allows determination of the date of seroconversion') is not the canonical dating marker (IgG avidity dates infection); distractors a/c/d clearly false but the keyed option is only loosely defensible, so held for adjudication rather than authored to a shaky positive fact.

questions.title: Romana sign is characteristic of Chagas' disease
questions.question: Romana sign is characteristic of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. African sleeping sickness produces a trypanosomal chancre at the tsetse-fly bite site, not the Romana sign.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) causes fever, splenomegaly and pancytopenia, not periorbital oedema.
explanations.D: Correct. Romana sign is unilateral painless periorbital (bipalpebral) oedema with conjunctivitis that appears when the reduviid (triatomine) bug deposits Trypanosoma cruzi at the conjunctiva, marking the portal of entry in acute Chagas' disease. It is the classic acute-phase sign of American trypanosomiasis. Its presence therefore points to Chagas' disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Malaria causes cyclical fever and haemolytic anaemia, not a periorbital entry-site sign.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Romana sign as the acute-phase sign of Chagas' disease.

questions.title: Chiclero ulcer typically affects the ear
questions.question: Chiclero ulcer typically affects:

explanations.A: Correct. Chiclero ulcer is the cutaneous leishmaniasis of Leishmania mexicana, seen in forest workers (chicleros) who harvest chicle gum, and it characteristically involves the pinna of the ear because that is the exposed site the sandfly bites. The lesion is chronic and can destroy the cartilage of the ear. Chiclero ulcer therefore typically affects the ear.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lower-limb lesions are typical of Leishmania major (rural wet-type), not chiclero ulcer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Facial oriental sore is typical of Leishmania tropica, not chiclero ulcer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The trunk is not the characteristic site of chiclero ulcer.

questions.learning_objective: Associate chiclero ulcer (L. mexicana) with lesions of the ear.

questions.title: Blood transfusion transmits toxoplasmosis via tachyzoites
questions.question: For toxoplasmosis the following is true:

options.A: Oocysts shed in cat faeces are directly infective
options.B: Blood transfusion transmits infection through tachyzoites
options.C: In man, bradyzoites released from ingested cysts initiate intestinal schizogony
options.D: Diagnosis in man is done through finding oocysts in stool

explanations.A: Incorrect. Freshly shed oocysts are unsporulated and non-infective; they must sporulate in the environment over 1-5 days before they become infective.
explanations.B: Correct. Tachyzoites are the rapidly dividing invasive stage that circulates in blood and body fluids during acute toxoplasmosis, so transfused blood and transplanted organs (and transplacental passage) can transmit infection through tachyzoites. This is why blood-borne transmission is recognised for Toxoplasma gondii. Transfusion transmitting infection through tachyzoites is therefore the true statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The enteroepithelial (schizogony/gametogony) cycle occurs only in the definitive cat host, not in man.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Oocysts are shed only by cats, so they are not found in human stool and are not used to diagnose human infection.

questions.learning_objective: State that toxoplasmosis is transfusion-transmissible via circulating tachyzoites.

questions.title: Pancytopenia is frequent in kala-azar
questions.question: Pancytopenia is frequently seen with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. African sleeping sickness causes fever, lymphadenopathy and CNS disease, not the marked pancytopenia of visceral leishmaniasis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chagas' disease causes myocarditis and megasyndromes, not pancytopenia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Malaria causes a haemolytic anaemia (and sometimes thrombocytopenia) but not the tri-lineage pancytopenia typical of kala-azar.
explanations.D: Correct. Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) causes massive splenomegaly with hypersplenism and heavy bone-marrow parasitism by amastigotes, which together suppress and destroy all three blood cell lines to produce pancytopenia (anaemia, leucopenia and thrombocytopenia). Pancytopenia is a defining haematological feature of kala-azar. It is therefore most frequently seen with kala-azar.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise pancytopenia as a feature of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar).

questions.title: Stool is not used to recover African trypanosomes
questions.question: A specimen that is not used for the recovery of African trypanosomes is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lymph node aspirate (Winterbottom sign nodes) is a standard specimen for recovering African trypanosomes.
explanations.B: Correct. African trypanosomes (Trypanosoma brucei gambiense and rhodesiense) are blood-and-tissue-fluid parasites found in blood, lymph node aspirate and, once the CNS is invaded, cerebrospinal fluid; they do not inhabit the gut and are never recovered from stool. Stool examination has no role in diagnosing sleeping sickness. A stool sample is therefore the specimen not used.
explanations.C: Incorrect. CSF is examined to stage sleeping sickness once the trypanosomes reach the central nervous system.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Blood is a primary specimen for detecting trypomastigotes of African trypanosomes.

questions.learning_objective: State that African trypanosomes are not recovered from stool.

questions.title: Animal inoculation is not used to diagnose malaria
questions.question: Animal inoculation is NOT used for diagnosis of:

explanations.A: Correct. Human malaria parasites are diagnosed by examining stained blood films and by antigen/PCR tests; there is no practical laboratory animal that supports the human Plasmodium species, so animal inoculation is not used. In contrast, mice and other rodents are used to amplify Toxoplasma, trypanosomes and Babesia. Animal inoculation is therefore not used for malaria.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mouse inoculation is a recognised method to isolate Toxoplasma gondii.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rats and mice are inoculated to recover African trypanosomes (especially T. b. rhodesiense).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hamsters and gerbils are inoculated to amplify Babesia for diagnosis.

questions.learning_objective: State that animal inoculation is not a diagnostic method for malaria.

questions.title: Montenegro test is negative in active kala-azar
questions.question: Which of the following items does not describe kala-azar?

options.B: Transmitted by the Phlebotomus sandfly species
options.C: Diagnosed in the active phase by the Montenegro test
options.D: Can be serologically diagnosed by ELISA

explanations.A: Incorrect. Kala-azar is indeed common in India (a classic endemic focus), so this statement does describe it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Visceral leishmaniasis is transmitted by Phlebotomus sandflies, so this statement does describe kala-azar.
explanations.C: Correct. The Montenegro (leishmanin) skin test measures cell-mediated immunity and is NEGATIVE during active kala-azar because the disease suppresses cellular immunity; it converts to positive only after cure. Therefore it cannot be used to diagnose active visceral leishmaniasis. This statement does not describe kala-azar and is the correct answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Kala-azar can be diagnosed serologically by ELISA (and rK39), so this statement does describe it.

questions.learning_objective: State that the Montenegro test is negative during active kala-azar.

questions.title: Amoebic liver abscess aspirate shows only trophozoites
questions.question: Aspirates from a liver amoebic abscess show:

explanations.A: Correct. Only the invasive trophozoite of Entamoeba histolytica reaches and destroys tissue, so aspirate from the wall of an amoebic liver abscess contains motile trophozoites (classically at the advancing margin), never cysts. Encystation occurs only in the intestinal lumen, not in tissue. The aspirate therefore shows trophozoites only.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pre-cyst stages form in the bowel lumen, not in the liver abscess.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cysts are produced only in the intestinal lumen and are not found in tissue or in the abscess.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cysts do not form in tissue, so trophozoites and cysts together are not seen in the aspirate.

questions.learning_objective: State that amoebic liver abscess aspirate contains only trophozoites.

questions.title: Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis occurs with L. aethiopica
questions.question: Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis occurs with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Leishmania tropica causes localised urban oriental sore, not diffuse cutaneous disease.
explanations.B: Correct. Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis is a rare anergic form in which a defective cell-mediated response allows non-ulcerating nodules to spread widely over the skin, and in the Old World it is caused by Leishmania aethiopica. The lesions teem with amastigotes and the leishmanin test is negative. Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis therefore points to L. aethiopica.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leishmania major causes rural wet-type localised cutaneous leishmaniasis, not the diffuse form.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Leishmania donovani causes visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), not diffuse cutaneous disease.

questions.learning_objective: Associate Old World diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis with L. aethiopica.

questions.title: Espundia occurs with L. braziliensis
questions.question: Espundia occurs with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Leishmania aethiopica causes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis, not espundia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. L. tropica and L. aethiopica cause cutaneous disease, not mucocutaneous espundia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. L. tropica and L. major cause localised cutaneous leishmaniasis, not espundia.
explanations.D: Correct. Espundia is mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, in which Leishmania braziliensis metastasises from a healed skin lesion to the naso-oropharyngeal mucosa and destroys the nasal septum and cartilage. This destructive mucosal spread is characteristic of the L. braziliensis (Viannia) complex. Espundia therefore occurs with L. braziliensis.

questions.learning_objective: Associate espundia (mucocutaneous leishmaniasis) with L. braziliensis.

questions.title: Sandfly transmits visceral leishmaniasis
questions.question: Sandfly is involved in the transmission of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sleeping sickness is transmitted by the tsetse fly (Glossina), not the sandfly.
explanations.B: Correct. All Leishmania species, including the L. donovani that causes visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), are transmitted by the bite of female phlebotomine sandflies (Phlebotomus in the Old World, Lutzomyia in the New World). The sandfly is the definitive/vector host in which promastigotes develop. Visceral leishmaniasis is therefore the sandfly-transmitted infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Babesiosis is transmitted by hard (ixodid) ticks, not the sandfly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Toxoplasmosis is acquired by ingesting oocysts or tissue cysts, not by an insect vector.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the sandfly as the vector of visceral leishmaniasis.

questions.title: Uta occurs with the L. braziliensis complex
questions.question: Uta (oriental sore-like lesions) occurs with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. L. tropica causes Old World urban oriental sore, not the New World uta of the Andes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. L. aethiopica causes diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis in East Africa, not uta.
explanations.C: Incorrect. L. major causes Old World rural cutaneous leishmaniasis, not uta.
explanations.D: Correct. Uta is a localised oriental-sore-like cutaneous leishmaniasis of the Peruvian Andean highlands caused by Leishmania peruviana, a member of the New World Leishmania braziliensis (Viannia) complex. Among the options it belongs to the L. braziliensis group. Uta therefore occurs with L. braziliensis.

questions.learning_objective: Associate Andean uta with the L. braziliensis (Viannia) complex.

questions.title: Balantidium coli has two differently shaped nuclei
questions.question: A protozoan with two differently shaped nuclei is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Giardia intestinalis has two nuclei, but they are identical in size and shape, not two different shapes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cryptosporidium parvum is a tiny coccidian and does not have two differently shaped nuclei.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The Entamoeba histolytica trophozoite has a single nucleus with a central karyosome.
explanations.D: Correct. Balantidium coli, the only ciliate that infects man, has two nuclei of different shape: a large kidney-shaped macronucleus that controls metabolism and a small round micronucleus concerned with reproduction. This dimorphic macronucleus-plus-micronucleus arrangement is a defining ciliate feature. Two differently shaped nuclei therefore identify Balantidium coli.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Balantidium coli by its dimorphic macronucleus and micronucleus.

questions.title: Weight loss and emaciation in kala-azar
questions.question: Weight loss and emaciation are usually reported with:

explanations.A: Correct. Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) is a chronic systemic infection with prolonged fever, massive splenomegaly and progressive wasting, so untreated patients become severely emaciated and cachectic. Weight loss and emaciation are classic constitutional features of the disease. They are therefore usually reported with kala-azar.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hookworm causes iron-deficiency anaemia from chronic blood loss rather than the marked emaciation of kala-azar.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Enterobiasis (pinworm) causes perianal pruritus and is usually otherwise asymptomatic, not wasting.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Trichostrongyliasis is usually a mild or subclinical intestinal infection, not a wasting illness.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise weight loss and emaciation as constitutional features of kala-azar.

questions.title: Leishmania major typically affects the lower limbs
questions.question: Leishmania major typically affects:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ear lesions are typical of chiclero ulcer (Leishmania mexicana), not L. major.
explanations.B: Correct. Leishmania major causes rural, zoonotic, wet-type cutaneous leishmaniasis, and because the sandfly bites exposed skin the ulcers typically appear on the lower limbs and other exposed extremities. The moist, rapidly ulcerating sores are characteristic of the species. L. major therefore typically affects the lower limbs.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Facial oriental sore is characteristic of the urban Leishmania tropica, not L. major.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The trunk is not the characteristic site of L. major lesions.

questions.learning_objective: Associate L. major cutaneous lesions with the lower limbs/exposed extremities.

questions.hold: ambiguous — 'solid immunity to reinfection' is conferred by recovery from ANY cutaneous leishmaniasis (L. major, L. tropica and L. mexicana are all options), so the single printed key B (L. tropica) is non-discriminating; L. major (option d) is the species classically used for leishmanization precisely because it gives solid immunity. Held for human adjudication.

questions.title: Intracellular evasion is not used by Hymenolepis nana
questions.question: Intracellular location is not a mode of immune evasion for:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Toxoplasma gondii survives inside a parasitophorous vacuole in host cells, using an intracellular location to evade immunity.
explanations.B: Correct. Hymenolepis nana is an intestinal cestode (tapeworm) whose adult and cysticercoid stages live in the gut lumen and villous mucosa, not inside host cells, so it cannot use an intracellular location as an immune-evasion strategy. That mechanism belongs to the intracellular protozoa. Hymenolepis nana is therefore the organism that does not evade immunity by an intracellular location.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Plasmodium vivax lives inside hepatocytes and red cells, an intracellular niche that shields it from antibody.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Trypanosoma cruzi multiplies as intracellular amastigotes inside host cells, an intracellular evasion strategy.

questions.learning_objective: Contrast the luminal cestode Hymenolepis nana with intracellular protozoa.

questions.title: Bone marrow is the specimen of choice for L. donovani
questions.question: The specimen of choice for the recovery of L. donovani is:

explanations.A: Correct. Leishmania donovani is a visceral parasite that concentrates in the reticuloendothelial organs, so bone marrow aspirate is the routine specimen of choice for demonstrating amastigotes, being both high-yield and far safer than splenic puncture. Amastigotes are sought inside macrophages of the marrow smear. Bone marrow aspirate is therefore the preferred specimen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lymph node aspirate is a lower-yield option and not the routine specimen of choice.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Skin biopsy is used for cutaneous leishmaniasis, not for visceral L. donovani.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Urine is not used to recover L. donovani amastigotes (though antigen tests exist).

questions.learning_objective: Identify bone marrow aspirate as the specimen of choice for visceral leishmaniasis.

questions.title: The trypanosomal chancre is relatively painless
questions.question: Regarding the trypanosomal chancre:

options.A: Caused by bite of triatomine bugs
options.D: After healing, the skin is back to normal

explanations.A: Incorrect. The trypanosomal chancre of African sleeping sickness forms at the bite of the tsetse fly (Glossina); triatomine (reduviid) bugs transmit American trypanosomiasis.
explanations.B: Correct. The trypanosomal chancre is an indurated inflammatory nodule that develops at the tsetse-fly bite site in African trypanosomiasis and is characteristically firm but relatively painless. It arises as local parasite multiplication provokes an inflammatory reaction before the parasites disseminate. Being a relatively painless indurated swelling is therefore the correct description.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The chancre is seen far more often in non-immune travellers than in the indigenous endemic population, in whom it is uncommon.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The chancre resolves over two to three weeks but typically leaves a residual scar or pigmentation, so the skin does not return fully to normal.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the trypanosomal chancre as a relatively painless indurated tsetse-bite nodule.

questions.title: Reactivated Chagas' disease causes meningoencephalitis
questions.question: Chagas' disease in the immunocompromised may show:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pneumonitis is not the characteristic reactivation manifestation of Chagas' disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chronic watery diarrhoea suggests coccidian infections such as cryptosporidiosis, not reactivated Chagas' disease.
explanations.C: Correct. In immunosuppressed patients (HIV/AIDS or transplant recipients) chronic Trypanosoma cruzi infection can reactivate, and the hallmark of reactivation is severe central nervous system disease, a necrotising meningoencephalitis (often with brain mass lesions), together with acute myocarditis. This CNS reactivation is characteristic of immunocompromised Chagas' disease. Meningoencephalitis is therefore the expected manifestation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Malabsorption is not a recognised reactivation feature of Chagas' disease.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise meningoencephalitis as reactivation Chagas' disease in the immunocompromised.

questions.title: Naegleria fowleri has amoeboid and flagellate forms
questions.question: Amoeboid and flagellate forms are found with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Entamoeba coli is a non-flagellated amoeba with trophozoite and cyst stages only.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Balantidium coli is a ciliate, not an amoeboflagellate.
explanations.C: Correct. Naegleria fowleri is an amoeboflagellate: its usual amoeboid trophozoite can transform, when placed in distilled/fresh water, into a transient pear-shaped biflagellate swimming form, and it also has a cyst stage. This ability to switch between amoeboid and flagellate forms is a defining feature. Amoeboid and flagellate forms therefore identify Naegleria fowleri.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Acanthamoeba has only trophozoite and cyst stages and no flagellate form.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Naegleria fowleri as an amoeboflagellate with a transient flagellate form.

questions.title: Septicaemic malaria disseminates to cause multi-organ failure
questions.question: The following is true regarding septicaemic malaria:

options.A: Severe headache, drowsiness, coma and death
options.B: Occurs due to immune complex deposition
options.C: Dissemination of the parasite to various organs, leading to multi-organ failure

explanations.A: Incorrect. Severe headache, drowsiness and coma describe cerebral malaria, not the septicaemic (algid) form.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Immune-complex deposition explains quartan malarial nephropathy, not septicaemic malaria.
explanations.C: Correct. Septicaemic (algid) malaria is severe Plasmodium falciparum disease in which heavy parasitaemia and widespread sequestration disseminate the effects of infection to many organs at once, producing circulatory collapse and multi-organ failure. It is the systemic, multi-organ presentation of complicated falciparum malaria. Dissemination leading to multi-organ failure is therefore the true statement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Severe falciparum disease, including this form, is closely related to cytoadherence and sequestration of infected red cells.

questions.learning_objective: Describe septicaemic malaria as multi-organ dissemination of severe falciparum disease.

questions.hold: negative-stem inconsistency — printed key marks statement b ('massive intravascular haemolysis of NON-parasitized red cells → blackwater fever') as the INCORRECT one, but the bank's own Q40 (option d, keyed true) accepts antibody haemolysins acting against RBC antigen as the blackwater-fever mechanism, i.e. immune haemolysis of (non-parasitized) red cells; labelling Q39-b incorrect is internally inconsistent, so held.

questions.title: Blackwater fever is not caused by IV fluid over-infusion
questions.question: The following is NOT true regarding blackwater fever:

options.A: Occurs in severely infected non-immune adults
options.B: Occurs due to over-infusion of I.V. fluids
options.C: It is often fatal due to renal failure
options.D: Antibodies acting as haemolysins against RBC antigen

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true statement). Blackwater fever indeed occurs in severely infected non-immune adults with Plasmodium falciparum, so this does not answer a NOT-true stem.
explanations.B: Correct. Blackwater fever is caused by sudden massive intravascular haemolysis with haemoglobinuria (black urine), not by over-infusion of intravenous fluids, so this statement is untrue and is the answer to the negative stem. The haemolysis, often quinine-related and immune-mediated, produces the dark urine and renal failure. Attributing blackwater fever to IV-fluid over-infusion is therefore the false statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect (a true statement). Blackwater fever is often fatal from acute renal failure, so this is true and does not answer the stem.
explanations.D: Incorrect (a true statement). Antibodies acting as haemolysins against red-cell antigen are part of the immune haemolytic mechanism, so this is true.

questions.learning_objective: State that blackwater fever results from haemolysis, not IV fluid over-infusion.

questions.title: Man is intermediate host only in malaria and toxoplasmosis
questions.question: Man is intermediate host only in:

explanations.A: Correct. The definitive host is the one harbouring the sexual cycle, so in malaria (sexual cycle in the female Anopheles mosquito) and toxoplasmosis (sexual enteroepithelial cycle in the cat) man harbours only the asexual stages and is therefore the intermediate host only. In the other infections listed man is not restricted to an intermediate-host role in this sense. Malaria and toxoplasmosis is therefore the correct pairing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. In the trypanosomiases man carries the trypomastigotes and is regarded as a host in which the sexual cycle does not clearly reside in an insect the same way, so this pairing does not fit the intermediate-host-only rule as malaria/toxoplasmosis does.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Only toxoplasmosis (cat definitive host) fits; leishmaniasis does not pair with it here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Only malaria (mosquito definitive host) fits; leishmaniasis does not complete the pairing.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that man is intermediate host only in malaria and toxoplasmosis.

questions.title: Eight-nucleate cyst (Entamoeba coli) needs no treatment
questions.question: The presence of a rounded cyst with eight nuclei in a stool sample requires:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The finding is diagnostic of a commensal, so the stool need not be repeated for this reason.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Nitazoxanide targets pathogens such as Cryptosporidium and Giardia, not a harmless commensal.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Metronidazole is reserved for pathogenic amoebiasis (Entamoeba histolytica), not for Entamoeba coli.
explanations.D: Correct. A rounded mature cyst containing eight nuclei is the cyst of Entamoeba coli, a non-pathogenic commensal of the large bowel, so its presence indicates only faecal-oral exposure and requires no treatment. Recognising the eight-nucleate cyst distinguishes harmless E. coli from the four-nucleate cyst of pathogenic E. histolytica. No treatment is therefore required.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the eight-nucleate cyst of Entamoeba coli as a commensal needing no treatment.

questions.hold: ambiguous — autofluorescent oocysts under UV are a feature of BOTH Cyclospora cayetanensis (option d, keyed) AND Cystoisospora belli (option a); two correct options with a single printed key, held per the module's dual-correct hold rule.

questions.title: Cryptosporidiosis biopsy shows meronts and gamonts
questions.question: Intestinal biopsy in cases of cryptosporidiosis may show:

explanations.A: Correct. Cryptosporidium parvum completes its whole life cycle in one host at the brush border of enterocytes in an intracellular but extracytoplasmic vacuole, so an intestinal biopsy shows the endogenous developmental stages, the asexual meronts (schizonts) and the sexual gamonts, studding the epithelial surface. These endogenous stages are what histology reveals. Meronts and gamonts are therefore the biopsy finding.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Merozoites and sporozoites are released motile stages, not what is typically identified on routine biopsy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thin- and thick-walled oocysts are the transmission forms shed in stool, demonstrated by staining, not the biopsy appearance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cryptosporidium oocysts are already sporulated (autoinfective) when passed, and oocysts are a stool finding, not the endogenous biopsy stages.

questions.learning_objective: State that cryptosporidiosis biopsy shows endogenous meronts and gamonts at the brush border.

questions.title: Anorexia and fatigue dominate cyclosporiasis
questions.question: The most prominent and consistent symptoms in cyclosporiasis are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Biliary disease is a feature of coccidian infection in the profoundly immunosuppressed, not the typical prominent symptom of cyclosporiasis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Some weight loss occurs, but marked cachexia is not the most consistent feature.
explanations.C: Correct. Cyclospora cayetanensis causes a prolonged, relapsing watery diarrhoea accompanied by strikingly prominent and consistent anorexia and profound fatigue, which are hallmark constitutional complaints of the illness. This marked fatigue-and-anorexia picture, often lasting weeks, is characteristic of cyclosporiasis. Anorexia and fatigue are therefore the most prominent and consistent symptoms.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cyclosporiasis causes non-bloody watery diarrhoea, not the dysentery and tenesmus of invasive colitis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify anorexia and fatigue as the prominent, consistent symptoms of cyclosporiasis.

questions.title: Blastocystis hominis is linked to irritable bowel syndrome
questions.question: Irritable bowel syndrome is linked to infection with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Entamoeba polecki is a rare intestinal amoeba and is not the organism linked to irritable bowel syndrome.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) causes chronic colitis and, when heavy, rectal prolapse, not irritable bowel syndrome.
explanations.C: Correct. Blastocystis hominis is a common intestinal protozoan that is frequently recovered from patients with irritable bowel syndrome, and it is associated with the abdominal pain, bloating and altered bowel habit of that functional syndrome. This clinical link between Blastocystis carriage and irritable bowel syndrome is well recognised. Blastocystis hominis is therefore the answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Strongyloides stercoralis causes larva currens and hyperinfection, not the irritable bowel syndrome association.

questions.learning_objective: Associate Blastocystis hominis with irritable bowel syndrome.
